title: 10 Lessons for Living a Better Life
author: Stoic Wisdoms
summary: Stoic Wisdoms begins by asking what a good life actually means, urging readers to write down their own answer and cross out whatever they want only because others would see them having it. The essay then draws ten lessons from Epictetus, Seneca, and the author's own experience. They include testing thoughts before obeying them, treating being right as a responsibility to be gentle rather than a license, holding first judgments of people loosely, and recognizing that disappointing others is not proof of wrongdoing. Further lessons say security never fully arrives, old self-descriptions are habits that can be changed, repeated actions matter more than intentions, and a single bad day is not a verdict on a life. The closing lessons point to ordinary days as the substance of a life and to loved ones as mortal, so attention should be given now. The piece works as a compact character-formation guide for anyone leading themselves before leading others.
points: Ask whether a recurring thought leads to an action you can take; if not, it is circling rather than thinking, and writing it down for the next day separates signal from weather.
Being right is a responsibility: say the true thing once, plainly, and stop, because extra sentences proving how right you were cost the relationship.
Disappointment from others is only a fault of yours if you broke a promise rather than an assumption, so repair the first and be kind but firm about the second.
Removing the one daily action that most contradicts your stated values is usually more effective than adding a new habit.
Small improvements to ordinary, repeated moments such as the morning hour or the walk home outweigh rare big events because most of life is lived on ordinary days.
quotes: A thought arrives, and because it arrived in your own head it comes with a kind of authority.
I have come to think that being right is a responsibility rather than a license, because the person who is right is the one who can afford to be gentle.
The Stoics put what other people think of you among the things outside your control, in the same list as your body and your property, and they did not mean that opinion does not matter.
Changing often begins with acting differently long before you feel different.
Intentions are pleasant to hold and cost nothing, which is why we have so many of them.
A small improvement in something you do three hundred times a year is worth more than a large one in something you do once.
A good life that has no bad days in it is not a life. It is a holiday brochure.
Love, in the end, is mostly attention, and attention is given in ordinary hours or not at all.
